analysis.one_liner: Restores employer-mandated birth control coverage that the Supreme Court let some corporations drop.
analysis.headline: The bill won majority support in the Senate — 56 senators in favor — but a procedural vote needing 60 failed, 56-43, and it never got an up-or-down vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Supreme Court's Hobby Lobby decision let some for-profit employers refuse to include birth control coverage in their employees' health plans. This bill would have overridden that decision by law: any employer offering a health plan would have to cover every service federal law requires, including contraception, with no religious exemption for for-profit companies. It also kept the existing exemptions for churches and religiously affiliated nonprofits. A procedural vote that needed 60 senators to start debate got only 56, and the bill died there.
analysis.who_benefits: Women employees whose employers object to contraception: the bill would have guaranteed them the full range of FDA-approved contraceptive methods and related counseling at no out-of-pocket cost, as the Affordable Care Act originally required [S2][S3]. The bill text cites that by 2013, 47 million women were covered by the contraceptive-coverage requirement and saved $483 million in out-of-pocket costs that year [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Employers that offer group health plans could no longer deny coverage of any health service federal law requires, including contraception, even after the Hobby Lobby decision [S2][S3].
The bill applies 'notwithstanding' the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, closing the legal door the Supreme Court opened for for-profit corporations [S2][S3].
It preserves the existing accommodation for houses of worship and religiously affiliated nonprofits, so the mandate targets for-profit companies, not religious institutions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: For-profit employers with religious objections would bear the cost of providing contraceptive coverage they currently may omit. The bill's own findings cite an industry study estimating that NOT covering contraception costs employers 15-17% more, because unplanned pregnancies drive up medical, absence, and productivity costs [S3]. Health insurers would continue administering the mandated benefit under the ACA rules [S3].

drawbacks.text: The strongest objection is that it overrides religious-liberty protections: by applying 'notwithstanding' the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, Congress would force family-owned businesses whose owners hold sincere objections to pay for contraception anyway [S3]. Supporters of the Hobby Lobby ruling argued owners' religious conscience should shield closely held companies from this mandate.

The bill is narrow: it restores coverage but leaves in place other state-level limits on contraception access, and its protections are only as durable as the ACA's preventive-services regulations, which agencies could change [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly 47 million women the contraceptive-coverage requirement touches, the benefit is concrete: no-copay birth control that Hobby Lobby-era exemptions took away. The cost falls mainly on a specific subset of employers with religious objections, and the bill spares churches and religious nonprofits. The tradeoff is a genuine conflict between employers' claimed religious conscience and employees' health coverage; the bill resolves it in favor of employees while keeping the religious-institution exemptions that existed before the Supreme Court decision.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate voted on whether to even start debating the bill — a vote that needed 60 senators — and got only 56, so the bill never came up for an actual up-or-down vote and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Patty Murray introduced the bill on July 9, 2014, two weeks after the Supreme Court's Hobby Lobby decision, with 46 cosponsors (45 Democrats and 1 independent) [S1][S4][S5].
The Senate moved almost immediately to consideration: the motion to proceed was made July 14 and a cloture motion — the vote that would have allowed debate to begin — was filed the same day [S5].
On July 16, 2014, cloture on the motion to proceed failed 56-43, short of the 60 needed; 51 of 53 Democrats and both independents voted yes, while 42 of 45 Republicans voted no [S6][S5].
No further action was taken, and the bill expired when the 113th Congress ended January 3, 2015 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that object to contraception keep the right, under the Hobby Lobby ruling, to omit birth control coverage from their health plans. The 43 senators who blocked the vote also avoided a floor debate on an override of the Supreme Court decision.

for.name: Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill two weeks after the Hobby Lobby decision and led the push to bring it to the floor.

for.name: 46 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 45 Democrats and 1 independent cosponsoring the bill
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction [S4]; 51 of 53 Democrats plus both independents then voted to advance it to debate [S6].

for.name: Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Made the motion to proceed and moved to reconsider after the cloture vote failed, trying to keep the bill alive.

against.name: 42 of 45 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on cloture on the motion to proceed, denying the 60 votes needed to begin debate on the bill.

against.name: 3 Senate Republicans
against.role: Republican senators who broke with their caucus
against.what_they_did: Voted yes on cloture, providing the only Republican support for starting debate.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly unanimous among Democrats (51 of 53) and independents (2 of 2); opposition was nearly unanimous among Republicans, with only 3 of 45 voting to advance the bill [S6].

industries.industry: For-profit employers with religious objections to contraception
industries.note: These companies gained the right to omit contraceptive coverage under the Hobby Lobby decision; the bill would have taken that right away by overriding the Religious Freedom Restoration Act for mandated benefits. Because their gain came at the expense of employees' coverage, their interest ran against workers'.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: The bill keeps the ACA's structure intact: coverage of preventive services, including contraception, continues to flow through employer-sponsored plans and insurers, who administer the mandate. It restores rather than disrupts the existing channel.
